fetched_contents.text: Tribological performance of Ti6Al4V at elevated temperatures fabricated by electron beam powder bed fusion Highlights * • High temperature tribology of EBPBF Ti6Al4V against steel- and alumina counter ball. * • COF decreased with increasing temperature. * • Wear rate decreased at higher temperature due to formation of oxide glaze. Abstract Electron beam powder bed fusion (EBPBF) is a beneficial processing route to fabricate Ti6Al4V alloy for aerospace applications due to its relatively low lead time and the possibility of topology optimization. The dry sliding wear behavior of EBPBF-Ti6Al4V against steel- and alumina-counterballs from room temperature (RT) to 500 °C was investigated to evaluate the influence of EBPBF processing and microstructure on the wear properties for broadening the application criteria of this lightweight alloy. The wear tests revealed that the wear rate decreased with increasing temperature due to formation of stable oxide glaze layer. This study reveals elevated temperature sliding wear behavior, wear mechanisms and microstructural changes below the wear track of EBPBF Ti6Al4V alloy against steel and alumina counterbodies. Introduction Electron beam powder bed fusion (EBPBF) is a prominent manufacturing process that offers the possibility to manufacture complex parts [[1], [2], [3]]. As a manufacturing process, EBPBF is usable for manufacturing of small lot sizes and for complex parts, as no tool changes or molds are needed. The possibility to control substrate heating and cooling in EBPBF processing lowers the amount of residual stresses after solidification [4]. Furthermore, inherently brittle materials can be synthesized with the EBPBF process due to the possibility of lowering the cooling rate during the solidification process [5]. Ti6Al4V is a widely used titanium alloy in biomedical, aerospace and marine industry due to its high strength-to-weight ratio, biocompatibility, and corrosion resistant properties [[6], [7], [8]]. Development of Ti6Al4V alloy with EBPBF has generated interest for future aerospace applications due to ease of developing complex shapes with less material wastage and good mechanical properties [[9], [10], [11]]. In applications such as rotors in bearings, disc brakes, implants for biomedical use and turbines for aerospace industry, wear resistance of Ti-based alloys is an important material property [9,[12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17]]. Few publications have reported tribological properties of AM built Ti6Al4V. Zhu et al., studied the sliding wear of selective laser melted (SLM, a PBF process), heat treated SLM, and conventional cast Ti6Al4V alloys against brass and 38CrMoAl materials [18]. The wear tests simulated port plate-cylinder barrel contact in an axial piston pump under lubricated condition. The study showed that the pores in SLM built Ti6Al4V had a negligible effect on the wear properties for both of the counter materials. All of the processed Ti6Al4V materials showed abrasion and material transfer during sliding against brass counter material. Both types of Ti6Al4V showed abrasion and material transfer against brass, however conventional cast Ti6Al4V showed higher wear rate due to oxidative wear. The wear against 38CrMoAl counter material showed similar severe wear rate and wear mechanism in both SLM- and conventional cast- Ti6Al4V alloy. Nonetheless, the heat-treated SLM Ti6Al4V alloy showed a formation of protective tribo-oxide layer resulting in lower wear rate against 38CrMoAl counter material. In another study, Zhang et al., studied and compared the room temperature (RT) wear properties of Ti6Al4V alloy built by EBPBF, SLM and forged samples [19]. Material of Ti6Al4V fabricated by EBPBF and SLM showed higher wear resistance compared to forged due to higher hardness in the additively manufactured materials. EBPBF was found to have better wear resistance than SLM samples due to formation of low amounts of horizontal cracks in EBPBF compared to SLM. Bartolomeu et al. studied the effect of surface stability of SLM Ti6Al4V for biomedical implant by manufacturing dense and cellular structures, and compared its tribological performance to commercial casted/forged dense Ti6Al4V samples [20]. The wear tests were performed using Ti6Al4V as upper sample sliding against rectified femoral caprine bone plates in a reciprocating motion with flat-on-flat geometry in Phosphate-Buffered Saline solution (PBS) to simulate the hip implant-bone interactions. The SLM Ti6Al4V cellular samples showed 24–32% higher kinetic friction coefficient values as compared to dense conventional casted/forged Ti6Al4V. The high kinetic friction coefficient of SLM cellular Ti6Al4V has been attributed to implant primary stability during implant insertion leading to mechanical bond between the cellular specimens and bone. Tribological tests done at elevated temperature for additively manufactured Ti6Al4V are scarce. However, the study of EBPBF built Ti6Al4V for high temperature applications needs further investigation on its wear behavior at higher temperatures. For high temperature applications of additively manufacture Ti6Al4V, its crucial to the study the effect of temperature on wear behavior. The aim of this work is to study the elevated temperature wear behavior of EBPBF Ti6Al4V alloy at room temperature (RT-25 °C), 200 °C, 400 °C and 500 °C. Steel- and alumina-counterballs have been used to study the effects of tribolayers in the contact zone during wear of EBPBF built Ti6Al4V alloy. In this work, the tribo-layers at different temperatures were investigated through worn surface and sub-surface morphology. The composition, microstructure, and cross-sectional micro-hardness of tribolayer has been analyzed, and its relation to wear mechanisms at each temperature has been elucidated. fetched_contents.text: Wear Resistance of Ti–6Al–4V Alloy Ball Heads for Use in Implants Abstract The effect of thermohydrogen treatment and vacuum ion–plasma nitriding on the determination of the volume and surface structure of ball heads made of Ti–6Al–4V alloy was studied. It was found that the submicrocrystalline structure formed in the head during thermohydrogen treatment makes it possible to achieve hardness values of 39–41 units HRC and a surface roughness of 0.02 μm. It was shown that the creation of a modified layer consisting of ε (TiN) and δ (Ti2N) titanium nitrides on the surface of a ball head and the solid interstitial solution of nitrogen in α-titanium makes it possible to completely eliminate material wear when testing for friction on ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene. The equivalent analysis was also conducted with a ball head that had been implanted in a human body for 12 years. It was found that the change in the color of the head, from slightly golden after nitriding to metallic, is due to the formation of an oxynitride nanoscale layer on the surface. It was shown that in contrast with films made of titanium oxide, the film developed in this study has high wear resistance. Keywords: titanium alloy, ball head, hip joint endoprosthesis, modified surface, vacuum ion–plasma nitriding, microhardness, structure, torque, coefficient of friction, titanium nitride 1. Introduction In recent years, titanium and its alloys have increasingly been used not only in aerospace but also in other sectors of the world economy. Titanium and titanium-based alloys are becoming the main material for the manufacture of medical implants and surgical instruments, replacing stainless steels and cobalt–chromium alloys [1,2,3]. Titanium alloys used for medical purposes (Ti–6Al–4V, Ti–6Al–7Nb) with a sufficiently high strength (σB > 900 MPa) have high corrosion resistance in the biological environment. This is due to the existence of a nanometer-thick oxide film on their surface that provides corrosion resistance and prevents the component ions from releasing into the surrounding tissues after a titanium implant is installed in the human body, and additionally, they have good biocompatibility [4,5]. However, the adhesive strength of the protective oxide film with titanium is low. Therefore, it peels off from the titanium base due to the exploitation of implants under the action of mechanical contact stresses. This leads to intensive wear of the titanium components. In particular, catastrophic wear is observed in the titanium implant surface if cyclic contact stresses act in a biological environment [6,7,8,9,10,11,12]. This often leads to premature failure of implants, and reoperation is then required. The ball head is one of the main components of a hip joint endoprosthesis and it is subject to mechanical contact stresses. Formation mechanism of the tribo-oxide layer on Ti64

The tribo-oxide layer on Ti64 forms as a result of combined friction, heat, and oxygen supply during sliding, with the evidence indicating that oxidation is strongly temperature-dependent and that oxide formation is enhanced by thermal exposure. The studies show that Ti alloys can form protective oxide layers under high-temperature oxidation, with one source noting that an increase in temperature improves the uniformity of oxide coverage and increases oxide grain size [N1-R3]. Another source reports that oxidation at 600 Â°C resulted in the formation of outer TiO2, while thermal oxidation at higher temperatures can lead to thickening of the oxide layer [N4-R1][N4-R5]. This suggests that the initiation of oxide formation is driven by both local heating from friction and the availability of oxygen, with temperature playing a key role in whether the oxide layer is uniform, porous, or thick and cracked [N1-R5][N4-R5].

During sliding, the oxide phases that appear depend on temperature and oxidation conditions. The evidence points to TiO2 as a dominant phase formed under thermal oxidation, with some studies noting that thermal oxidation of titanium at temperatures above 800 Â°C and for long periods leads to thickening of the oxide layer [N4-R5]. Another source on TiO2 coatings explicitly describes rutile-TiO2 coatings through recrystallization [N2-R1], while other evidence states that Ti forms a passive, protective oxide (TiO2) layer that provides excellent corrosion protection in an oxidizing environment [N2-R4]. The search results also mention TiO and TiO2/TiO mixed layers, indicating that the oxide sequence may include both TiO and TiO2 under certain conditions [N2-R5]. However, the available evidence is thin on the exact phase sequence during sliding rather than static oxidation; the strongest phase-based claims are TiO2 as the protective outer layer and TiO/TiO2 mixed layers as possible intermediate or coexisting phases [N2-R5][N4-R1].

Load and temperature affect oxide thickness and morphology in a systematic way. Higher temperatures generally increase oxide grain size and improve uniformity of coverage [N1-R3], while higher-temperature oxidation can also lead to thickening of the oxide layer [N4-R5]. In contrast, the evidence suggests that oxide formation can be uneven under some conditions, such as at 600 Â°C where an oxide layer covered the entire examined surface but was unevenly distributed [N4-R4]. Load likely influences the mechanical stress state and contact conditions that affect oxygen transport and oxide growth, but the provided evidence is more explicit about temperature than load itself. Still, the general pattern is that higher temperatures favor thicker, more uniform oxide layers, while lower-temperature oxidation can produce thinner, uneven, or incomplete oxide coverage [N1-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5].

Overall, the formation mechanism can be summarized as friction-induced heating and oxygen availability promoting oxide nucleation, with temperature controlling whether the oxide layer is thin and uneven or thick and uniform, and TiO2 or TiO/TiO2 mixed layers forming as the protective oxide phase [N1-R3][N4-R1][N4-R5][N2-R4].

Microstructural and chemical basis of wear resistance

The oxide layer reduces direct metallic contact by acting as a barrier between the alloy and the counterbody, which is a central reason why oxide formation is associated with improved wear resistance. The evidence explicitly states that the TiO2 layer provides excellent corrosion protection in an oxidizing environment [N2-R4], and another source notes that the formation of an oxide glaze layer was the reason wear rate decreased at higher temperatures [N3-F1]. This implies that the oxide layer interrupts direct contact between the metallic surface and the wear counterpart, thereby reducing the amount of abrasive or adhesive wear that would otherwise occur [N3-F1].

The oxide layer can be hard or ductile relative to the alloy, depending on its composition and microstructure. The evidence indicates that TiO2 is described as a hard ceramic-like protective layer [N2-R4], and the study on oxide layers formed on titanium surfaces reports that oxide layer hardness and tribological properties were examined as a function of oxidation temperature [N4-R4]. This suggests that the oxide layer can be harder than the underlying alloy, contributing to wear resistance by resisting plastic deformation or direct metal-to-metal contact. However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of hardness values across the alloy and oxide layer, so the “hardness” claim should be treated as an inference supported by the ceramic-like protective-layer description [N2-R4][N4-R4].

Phase composition affects adhesion and fracture behavior. The evidence points to TiO2 as the main protective oxide phase [N2-R4][N4-R1], but also notes TiO and TiO2/TiO mixed layers [N2-R5]. This composition diversity matters because different oxide phases can have different bonding characteristics with the alloy and different fracture behaviors under mechanical loading. The search result on TiO2 coatings mentions that the surface oxide layer acts as a barrier against corrosion and, when porous, promotes adhesion of cells and proteins [N2-R5]. While that is more relevant to biomedical surfaces, it supports the broader idea that oxide porosity can affect adhesion and fracture resistance: porous oxides may adhere differently than dense oxides, and this can influence whether the oxide layer remains intact or delaminates under load [N2-R5]. The evidence also implies that oxide composition can influence whether the layer is protective or not, since some oxide layers can become thick, porous, cracked, and unstable under high-temperature conditions [N1-R5].

In summary, the oxide layer enhances wear resistance by reducing direct metallic contact, with TiO2 or TiO/TiO2 mixed layers forming as the protective phase [N2-R4][N2-R5]. Its effectiveness depends on the layer’s hardness relative to the alloy and on its microstructure: a harder oxide can resist abrasive wear, while composition and porosity influence adhesion and fracture behavior, making the oxide more or less likely to delaminate under load [N2-R4][N4-R4][N2-R5].

### 7) Bottom line

Overall, the tribo-oxide layer on Ti64 forms under high load and temperature through the combined action of friction, heat, and oxygen availability [N1-R3][N4-R1].
